Naturallyoccurring phytosterols in lipid nanoparticles induce rigidity reshape and endosome retention to enhance intracellular mRNA processing.

This study shows that replacing cholesterol in mRNA lipid nanoparticles with naturally occurring phytosterols bearing C-24 alkyl substitutions changes the particles' mechanical rigidity and causes them to be retained longer in endosomes, which improves intracellular mRNA processing and transfection efficiency. The work maps structure-activity relationships between sterol chemistry and LNP performance, offering design rules for next-generation mRNA delivery systems.

Mechanisms of Hofmeister ion effects on protein properties and their applications in food protein processing: A review.

This review synthesizes the mechanisms by which Hofmeister series ions—especially anions—modulate protein properties through effects on water structure and direct ion-protein interactions. It then surveys applications of these ion-specific effects in food protein processing, including extraction, gelation, emulsion stabilization, and structural modification. The authors highlight that the Hofmeister effect is a multifaceted phenomenon with practical relevance for controlling protein functionality in food systems.

Cryo-EM reveals a transmembrane allosteric site and activation mechanism for the SERCA calcium pump.

Using cryo-EM, the authors determined structures of the SERCA calcium pump bound to two chemically distinct small-molecule activators (CDN1163 and UM-52) at 2.6 Å and 3.1 Å resolution. They identify a previously unknown allosteric binding site within the transmembrane domain and propose a mechanism by which these compounds enhance SERCA activity. This provides the first structural basis for pharmacological SERCA activation, relevant to cardiovascular and metabolic disease.

From passive deposition to signal-guided targeting: a functional outer layer enables preferential stomatal colonization by a microbial herbicide.

This paper addresses two bottlenecks in foliar-applied microbial herbicides: rapid loss of viability under environmental stress and passive, random deposition that limits contact with host entry sites. The authors describe a functional outer layer that converts passive deposition into signal-guided targeting, enabling preferential colonization of stomata by the microbial herbicide. This represents a formulation/engineering strategy to improve the efficacy and reliability of biological weed-control agents.

Biophysically grounded deep learning improves protein-protein ΔΔG prediction.

The authors show that standard train-test splits of the SKEMPI2 protein-protein binding affinity dataset leak homology information, inflating the apparent accuracy of AI ΔΔG predictors; all tested models degrade under a stringent chain-level 60% identity split. They introduce ProtBFF, a modular framework that fuses five residue-level biophysical descriptors with pretrained protein embeddings via cross-embedding attention, improving ΔΔG prediction under leakage-controlled evaluation.

CoEVFold suite: User friendly pipelines to visually represent protein coevolution.

The authors present CoEVFold, a user-friendly software suite for identifying and visualizing coevolutionary signals in protein multiple sequence alignments. It implements direct coupling analysis algorithms derived from GREMLIN, making the core signal underlying deep-learning protein structure prediction accessible to non-specialists. The suite provides pipelines to visually represent coevolving residue pairs, filling a gap in accessible tools for coevolution analysis.

Advances in photothermal nanozymes: from rational design to multifunctional theranostic platforms.

This review surveys photothermal nanozymes, materials that combine enzyme-like catalytic activity with light-driven heating, and describes how localized hyperthermia accelerates reaction kinetics and improves substrate access to produce synergistic therapeutic effects. It organizes the field with a composition-based classification covering noble metals, transition metal compounds, carbon materials, Prussian blue analogues, single-atom catalysts, and metal-organic frameworks, and highlights design strategies and multifunctional theranostic applications.

AlphaFold models of host-pathogen interactions elucidate the prevalence and structural modes of molecular mimicry.

This paper benchmarks AlphaFold2 and AlphaFold3 for predicting structures of host-pathogen protein-protein interactions, finding that accurate models can be retrieved by ranking on modelling confidence despite overall limitations. Using these models, the authors survey thousands of known host-pathogen PPIs to assess how prevalent molecular mimicry is and to characterize the structural modes by which pathogen proteins imitate host interfaces, including evidence of convergent evolution of interaction surfaces.

Large-scale analysis of AlphaFold structures reveals organism-specific physicochemical signatures.

The authors analyzed physicochemical properties across 373,779 high-confidence AlphaFold-predicted protein structures and found systematic organism-specific differences. These differences are strong enough to recover major features of the tree of life, and the signal persists even when restricting to eukaryotic proteins. This demonstrates that predicted structural data can capture evolutionary and organismal signatures at scale.

Enhancing Enzyme pH Adaptation for Industrial Biocatalysis: From Sequence-Dependent Engineering to Sequence-Independent Stabilization.

This review examines how enzymes can be engineered to function outside their narrow natural pH optima, a key limitation in industrial biocatalysis. It distinguishes sequence-dependent strategies, which involve mutating specific ionizable residues, from sequence-independent stabilization approaches that improve overall robustness without targeting individual positions. The paper aims to guide rational design of pH-tolerant enzymes for sectors like detergents, textiles, and biorefineries.

Structure-based computational screening of cyclotides as putative CYP19A1-binding scaffolds for modulation of estrogen biosynthesis in adenomyosis.

This study used computational docking and molecular dynamics to screen cyclotide peptides as potential binders of CYP19A1 (aromatase), the enzyme responsible for local estrogen production in adenomyosis. The authors identify cyclotide scaffolds that interact favorably with the enzyme's active site, proposing them as starting points for developing estrogen-modulating therapeutics. The work is entirely in silico with no experimental validation.
